Answer: (C) American Institute of Certified Public Accountants.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The relation between book-keeping, accounting and accountancy is that-

options.A: accounting is a subset of book-keeping, and book-keeping in turn is a part of accountancy
options.B: book-keeping is a subset of accountancy, and accountancy in turn is a part of accounting
options.C: book-keeping is a subset of accounting, and accounting in turn is a part of accountancy
options.D: accountancy is a subset of accounting, and accounting in turn is a part of book-keeping

answer_html:
Answer: (C) book-keeping is a subset of accounting, and accounting in turn is a part of accountancy.

Book-keeping is defined by Carter as the science and art of correctly recording in books of accounts all those business transactions that result in transfer of money or money's worth, and it is a concept narrower than accounting. Accountancy refers to the entire body of the theory and practice of accounting and is a concept wider than accounting. Thus book-keeping is a subset of accounting, and accounting is a part of accountancy.

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Conceptual, Legal, Institutional and Regulatory.

The framework of accounting has four pillars, namely the Conceptual framework, the Legal framework, the Institutional framework and the Regulatory framework. Together these four provide the foundation on which accounting, and more specifically corporate accounting, is based in India.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Which of the following is a function of the Conceptual framework of accounting?

options.A: It determines the manner in which listed entities report to the market and the manner in which banks account for non-performing assets
options.B: It guides on the qualitative characteristics that financial statements must possess and assists preparers in developing consistent accounting policies where no standard applies
options.C: It prescribes the form and contents of the financial statements to be prepared by every class of business organisation carrying on activity in India
options.D: It issues the pronouncements which entities are obliged to follow while measuring and presenting the elements of their financial statements

answer_html:
Answer: (B) It guides on the qualitative characteristics that financial statements must possess and assists preparers in developing consistent accounting policies where no standard applies.

The Conceptual Framework is a body of interrelated objectives and fundamentals. It states the objectives of General-Purpose Financial Reporting and guides on the qualitative characteristics that the financial statements must possess. It also assists preparers to develop consistent accounting policies when no accounting standard applies to a particular transaction or event, or when a standard allows a choice of accounting policy. Prescribing the form and contents of financial statements is the work of the Legal framework, issuing pronouncements is the work of the Institutional framework, and the matters in Option (A) belong to the Regulatory framework.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: As regards the statutes governing the different forms of business organisation-

options.A: sole proprietorships are the least regulated and normally have no specific legislation governing accounting requirements, while partnership firms are regulated by the Partnership Act, 1932 and also the Contract Act, 1872
options.B: sole proprietorships are governed by the Income Tax Act, 1961 in every case, while partnership firms are regulated by the Partnership Act, 1932 to the exclusion of the Contract Act, 1872
options.C: sole proprietorships and partnership firms are alike governed by the Partnership Act, 1932, the difference between them lying only in the number of persons carrying on the business
options.D: sole proprietorships are the least regulated and are outside every statute, while partnership firms are regulated by the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 in all their operations

answer_html:
Answer: (A) sole proprietorships are the least regulated and normally have no specific legislation governing accounting requirements, while partnership firms are regulated by the Partnership Act, 1932 and also the Contract Act, 1872.

Sole proprietorship organisations are the least regulated in India and normally do not have any specific legislation to govern accounting requirements, though where their annual turnover exceeds a certain limit they may be subject to other legislation such as the Income Tax Act, 1961. Partnership firms are regulated by the Partnership Act, 1932 and also the Contract Act, 1872, and where the partnership contract has no clear provision the Partnership Act, 1932 decides on the sharing of profits and losses and on partners' claims such as remuneration and interest on loan. Operations of LLPs, including some aspects of accounting, are governed by the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The principle 'Anticipate no profit, but provide for all possible losses' is the basis of the convention of-

options.A: Consistency
options.B: Materiality
options.C: Full disclosure
options.D: Conservatism

answer_html:
Answer: (D) Conservatism.

The convention of conservatism is based on the principle that one should anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses. It is based on the policy of playing safe in regard to showing profit, and its main objective is to show minimum profit, because if profit is shown as more than the actual, it may lead to distribution of dividend out of capital and thereby to a reduction in the capital of the enterprise.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Under the realisation concept, revenue is treated as having been realised when-

options.A: the expenses relating to the goods concerned have been incurred and recorded
options.B: the legal right to receive money has been created, as by the sale of goods or services
options.C: the order from the customer has been received and accepted by the business
options.D: the goods have been manufactured and are lying ready in the godown for sale

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the legal right to receive money has been created, as by the sale of goods or services.

The realisation concept states that revenue from any business transaction should be included in the accounting records only when it is realised, and the term realisation means creation of a legal right to receive money. Selling goods is realisation, receiving an order is not. Revenue is accordingly said to have been realised when cash has been received or the right to receive cash on the sale of goods or services, or both, has been created.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The reason why cash introduced by the proprietor is recorded as a liability of the business is the-

options.A: money measurement concept
options.B: going concern concept
options.C: convention of full disclosure
options.D: business entity concept

answer_html:
Answer: (D) business entity concept.

The business entity concept assumes that, for accounting purposes, the business enterprise and its owners are two separate independent entities, so that the business and personal transactions of the owner are kept separate. When the owner invests money in the business it is therefore recorded as a liability of the business to the owner, and when the owner takes away cash or goods from the business for personal use it is not treated as a business expense.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The concept by which the infinite life of an organisation is split into smaller periods of equal duration, such as a quarter, half-year or year, is the-

options.A: matching or expense recognition concept
options.B: accrual or mercantile basis concept
options.C: periodicity or accounting period concept
options.D: going concern or continuity of business concept

answer_html:
Answer: (C) periodicity or accounting period concept.

The periodicity or accounting period concept assumes that the infinite life of an organisation can be split into smaller periods of equal duration such as a quarter, half-year or year. It is because of this concept that the operating results are ascertained for a specific period and the financial position is reflected, through the balance sheet, at regular intervals.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The determination of expenses for an accounting period is based on the concept of-

options.A: Matching
options.B: Objectivity
options.C: Materiality
options.D: Periodicity

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Matching.

The matching concept states that revenues and expenses must be recorded at the same time at which they are incurred, so that the revenues earned during an accounting period are matched with the expenses incurred during that period. It is for the application of this concept that several adjustments are made for prepaid expenses, accrued incomes and the like, since the operating result of an accounting period can be measured only when incomes are compared with the related expenses incurred.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A machine was purchased for ₹5,00,000, ₹1,000 was spent on transporting it to the factory site and ₹2,000 on its installation, its market price at the year end being ₹5,50,000. The amount at which the machine will be recorded in the books is-
answer_html:
Answer: (B) ₹5,03,000.

The cost concept states that all assets are recorded in the books of accounts at their purchase price, which includes the cost of acquisition, transportation and installation, and not at market price. The machine is therefore recorded at ₹5,00,000 plus ₹1,000 plus ₹2,000, that is ₹5,03,000, and this is also known as historical cost. The market price of ₹5,50,000 in Option (D) is disregarded.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The fundamental accounting equation in which the dual aspect concept is commonly expressed is-

options.A: Liabilities = Assets + Capital
options.B: Assets = Liabilities + Capital
options.C: Assets = Liabilities − Capital
options.D: Capital = Assets + Liabilities

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

The dual aspect concept is the foundation or basic principle of accounting and provides the very basis of recording business transactions in the books of accounts. It assumes that every transaction has a dual effect, that is, it affects two accounts on their respective opposite sides, and the duality concept is commonly expressed in terms of the fundamental accounting equation that assets equal liabilities plus capital.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The advantage claimed for the money measurement concept is that-

options.A: the results of the business are ascertained without any need to split its life into periods
options.B: different types of transactions can be recorded as homogeneous entries with money as the common denominator
options.C: the value of the assets shown in the books is kept in agreement with their current market worth
options.D: the qualitative attributes of the enterprise are brought on record along with the quantitative ones

answer_html:
Answer: (B) different types of transactions can be recorded as homogeneous entries with money as the common denominator.

A business transaction is recorded only if it can be expressed in terms of money, and the advantage of this concept is that different types of transactions can be recorded as homogeneous entries with money as the common denominator. A business may own cash, raw material, vehicles and computers, and unless each of these is expressed in terms of money the assets owned by the business cannot be found out; expressed in the common measure of money they can be added or subtracted to find the combined effect.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A firm has valued its closing inventory at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower, and has followed the same basis in each of the last five years. The two principles respectively reflected in the basis of valuation and in its repetition year after year are-

options.A: the cost concept and the convention of materiality
options.B: the convention of conservatism and the convention of consistency
options.C: the convention of consistency and the convention of conservatism
options.D: the convention of materiality and the convention of full disclosure

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the convention of conservatism and the convention of consistency.

Valuing inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value reflects the convention of conservatism, since it anticipates no profit but provides for a possible loss. Following the same basis year after year reflects the convention of consistency, which means that the same accounting principles should be used for preparing financial statements year after year, for a meaningful conclusion can be drawn from the financial statements of the same enterprise only when the accounting policies and practices followed are uniform and consistent over a period of time.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The convention which requires that only important and relevant information be supplied to users, and the convention which requires full, fair and adequate disclosure of accounting information, are respectively the conventions of-

options.A: materiality and full disclosure
options.B: full disclosure and materiality
options.C: conservatism and materiality
options.D: consistency and full disclosure

answer_html:
Answer: (A) materiality and full disclosure.

The convention of materiality states that, to make financial statements meaningful, only material facts, that is important and relevant information, should be supplied to the users of accounting information, and a material fact means information which will influence the decision of its user, its materiality depending on its nature and the amount involved. The convention of full disclosure requires that all material and relevant facts concerning the financial statements be fully disclosed, full referring to complete and detailed presentation, fair to equitable treatment of users and adequate to a sufficient set of information.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The accrual concept is significant because-

options.A: cash transactions alone affect owner's equity, credit transactions creating no obligation towards or by the business
options.B: every transaction affects two accounts on their respective opposite sides and must be recorded at two places
options.C: the business is assumed to continue in operation for a longer period of time and has no intention of curtailing operations
options.D: where credit transactions exist, revenues are not the same as cash receipts and expenses are not the same as cash paid during the period

answer_html:
Answer: (D) where credit transactions exist, revenues are not the same as cash receipts and expenses are not the same as cash paid during the period.

The accrual concept is based on the recognition of both cash and credit transactions. In a cash transaction the owner's equity is instantly affected as cash is either received or paid, whereas in a credit transaction a mere obligation towards or by the business is created. Since credit transactions generally exist, revenues are not the same as cash receipts and expenses are not the same as cash paid during the period. Option (B) states the dual aspect concept and Option (C) the going concern concept.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Which of the following is an event but not a transaction?

options.A: Investment of capital in the business by the owner
options.B: Purchase of goods by the business for resale
options.C: Payment of remuneration to the employees
options.D: Appointment of a new manager by the business

answer_html:
Answer: (D) Appointment of a new manager by the business.

A transaction is an event which can be expressed in monetary terms and brings a change in the financial position of a business unit. Investing capital, purchasing goods for resale and paying remuneration to employees are all transactions, since they lead to a change in the financial position. Using a new material in production or appointing a new manager are only events, as they do not change the financial position of the entity.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A capital expenditure is characterised by the fact that-

options.A: it is non-recurring in nature and its benefit is consumed over more than one accounting period
options.B: it is recurring in nature and its benefit is consumed over more than one accounting period
options.C: it is non-recurring in nature and its benefit is consumed within a single accounting period
options.D: it is recurring in nature and its benefit is consumed within a single accounting period

answer_html:
Answer: (A) it is non-recurring in nature and its benefit is consumed over more than one accounting period.

A capital expenditure is one the benefit from which can be enjoyed over a number of accounting periods. Its characteristics are that the amount involved is generally large, the benefit accruing from it is consumed over more than one accounting period, it is non-recurring in nature, and it results in an increase in the value of fixed assets. Option (D) states the characteristics of a revenue expenditure.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Capital expenditure and revenue expenditure are respectively-

options.A: reflected in the Balance Sheet and debited to the Income Statement
options.B: debited to the Income Statement and reflected in the Balance Sheet
options.C: reflected in the Balance Sheet and credited to the Income Statement
options.D: credited to the Income Statement and reflected in the Balance Sheet

answer_html:
Answer: (A) reflected in the Balance Sheet and debited to the Income Statement.

An expenditure of a capital nature is not written off completely against the income of the accounting period in which it is acquired but is capitalised, that is, recorded as an asset, and is reflected in the Balance Sheet. An expenditure of a revenue nature is charged as an expense against the profit of the accounting period in which it is incurred and is debited to the Income Statement.

question_html: A machine is bought for ₹5,00,000, ₹20,000 is paid as transportation charges and ₹40,000 as installation charges. The amount to be treated as capital expenditure is-
answer_html:
Answer: (D) ₹5,60,000.

Any expenditure incurred to put an asset into working condition is a capital expenditure and is added to the cost of the asset. The total cost of the machine therefore comes to ₹5,00,000 plus ₹20,000 plus ₹40,000, that is ₹5,60,000. On the same principle, where a building is purchased for ₹1,00,000 and ₹5,000 is spent on registration and stamp duty, the capital expenditure on the building stands at ₹1,05,000.

options.B: revenue expenditure and revenue expenditure
options.C: capital expenditure and revenue expenditure

Capital losses arising out of the sale of fixed assets generally appear in the Income Statement, being deducted from net profit, while other capital losses are adjusted against reserves of a capital nature; revenue losses such as discount allowed for prompt payment and bad debt loss are transferred to the Income Statement.

On 20 October ₹3,960 was received from him and ₹40 allowed as discount, and on 31 October ₹9,800 was received in full settlement of his account. The discount allowed on 31 October is-

options.C: Nil

answer_html:
Answer: (D) ₹200.

The debit side of Raman's account totals ₹4,000 plus ₹10,000, that is ₹14,000. Against this, cash of ₹3,960 and discount of ₹40 on 20 October and cash of ₹9,800 on 31 October account for ₹13,800, and as the account is settled in full the closing balance is nil. The discount allowed on 31 October is therefore the balancing figure of ₹14,000 less ₹13,800, that is ₹200.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Under the sub-division of the ledger, the ledger in which all transactions relating to assets and liabilities are recorded is the-

options.A: Private Ledger, which together with the Nominal Ledger forms the General Ledger
options.B: Nominal Ledger, which together with the Private Ledger forms the General Ledger
options.C: Personal Ledger, which together with the Creditors' Ledger forms the Debtors' Ledger
options.D: Impersonal Ledger, which together with the Personal Ledger forms the Nominal Ledger

answer_html:
Answer: (A) Private Ledger, which together with the Nominal Ledger forms the General Ledger.

The ledger is divided into the Personal Ledger, comprising the Debtors' Ledger and the Creditors' Ledger, and the Impersonal Ledger, comprising the Cash Book and Bank Book and the General Ledger. The General Ledger, in which all transactions relating to real accounts, nominal accounts and personal accounts other than trade debtors and trade creditors are recorded, is further divided into the Nominal Ledger, where transactions relating to incomes and expenses are recorded, and the Private Ledger, where transactions relating to assets and liabilities are recorded.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A cash book is-

options.A: a journal alone, the cash account being separately maintained in the general ledger
options.B: a ledger account alone, the entries being first passed in the journal proper
options.C: neither a journal nor a ledger, being merely a memorandum record of cash movements
options.D: both a journal and a ledger account, and is therefore also called a journalised ledger

answer_html:
Answer: (D) both a journal and a ledger account, and is therefore also called a journalised ledger.

A cash book is both a journal as well as a ledger account. It is a journal or book of original entry since transactions are recorded in it for the first time from the source documents, and it is also a ledger account in the sense that it is designed in the form of a Cash Account, recording cash receipts on the debit side and cash payments on the credit side. Because it simultaneously performs both functions it is also called a journalised ledger.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The letter 'C' is written on both sides in the Ledger Folio column of a double column cash book to denote-

options.A: a contra entry, such as the deposit of cash into bank or the withdrawal of cash from bank
options.B: a cash discount allowed to a customer at the time of settling his account in full
options.C: a cheque which has been received from a customer but not yet deposited into the bank
options.D: a casting of the cash and bank columns which has been checked and found correct

answer_html:
Answer: (A) a contra entry, such as the deposit of cash into bank or the withdrawal of cash from bank.

A double column cash book with cash and bank columns side by side gives rise to the contra entry. When any transaction takes place involving both Bank A/c and Cash A/c, the posting happens on both sides of the same book, examples being the deposit of cash into bank and the withdrawal of cash from bank. For recording such a transaction the letter 'C' is written on both sides in the Ledger Folio column.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: In a triple column cash book, the discount columns-

options.A: are balanced only at the end of the accounting year and not at the end of each month
options.B: are never balanced, their aggregate figures being directly posted to the respective ledger accounts
options.C: are balanced in the same manner as the cash and bank columns and the net figure carried down
options.D: record discount received on the debit side and discount allowed on the credit side of the book

answer_html:
Answer: (B) are never balanced, their aggregate figures being directly posted to the respective ledger accounts.

A triple column cash book has three columns on each side, namely Cash, Bank and Discount. The discount column on each side indicates two different types of discount, discount allowed on the debit side and discount received on the credit side. This is why the discount columns in a triple column cash book are never balanced, but their aggregate figures are directly posted to the respective ledger accounts.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A bank reconciliation statement is-

options.A: an account forming part of the double entry system, prepared for a period by the bank
options.B: a statement and not an account, prepared for a particular day by the entity holding the account

answer_html:
Answer: (B) a statement and not an account, prepared for a particular day by the entity holding the account.

A bank reconciliation statement is just a statement and not an account, and it is not a part of the double entry book keeping system. It is prepared for a particular day and not for a period, at regular intervals according to the requirement of the company, and it is prepared by an entity which has an account with a bank; a bank does not prepare it. In a single column cash book only one amount column is maintained on each side, to record transactions settled in liquid cash only. It is usually maintained by small organisations without access to any bank account, and also by an organisation which keeps a separate Bank A/c in its ledger. subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Under the imprest system of petty cash-

options.A: a pre-decided amount is given in lump sum to the petty cashier, who seeks reimbursement only when the whole of it has been spent
options.B: the petty cashier draws money from the bank as and when a petty expense arises, no float being placed at his disposal at all
options.C: the petty cashier is given an amount equal to the actual petty expenses of the preceding period at the close of every month
options.D: the total petty expenses for a period are estimated beforehand and advanced to the petty cashier, who is later reimbursed the exact amount spent

answer_html:
Answer: (D) the total petty expenses for a period are estimated beforehand and advanced to the petty cashier, who is later reimbursed the exact amount spent.

Under the imprest system the total amount of petty expenses for a particular period is estimated beforehand, and this amount, referred to as imprest cash or imprest float, is advanced by the principal cashier to the petty cashier. At the end of the fixed period the petty cashier submits a statement of petty cash and the chief cashier remits an amount equal to the total petty expenses incurred, so that at the beginning of the next period the petty cashier again has the same amount of imprest cash. Option (A) describes the ordinary system.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: Where the reconciliation is started with the favourable balance as per the Cash Book, cheques issued but not presented for payment are-

options.A: deducted, while cheques deposited but not yet cleared are added
options.B: added, and cheques deposited but not yet cleared are also added
options.C: deducted, and cheques deposited but not yet cleared are also deducted
options.D: added, while cheques deposited but not yet cleared are deducted

answer_html:
Answer: (D) added, while cheques deposited but not yet cleared are deducted.

Cheques issued but not presented in the bank have already been credited in the cash book but not yet debited by the bank, so the pass book shows the higher figure and the amount is added when starting from the balance as per the cash book. Cheques deposited in the bank but not cleared have already been debited in the cash book but not yet credited by the bank, so the amount is deducted. When the reconciliation starts from an overdraft as per the cash book the treatment of each is reversed.

case_facts_html:
The Cash Book of M/s Adarsh Trading for September 2023 showed opening balance ₹1,407, receipts ₹15,073, payments ₹15,520 and a closing balance carried down of ₹960.

On investigation it was found that (a) bank charges of ₹35 were not entered in the Cash Book, (b) a cheque of ₹47 issued to a supplier was entered by mistake as a receipt in the Cash Book, (c) a cheque of ₹18 was returned by the bank marked 'refer to drawer' but was not entered in the Cash Book, and (d) the balance brought forward in September 2023 should have been ₹1,470.

It was further found that (e) cheques paid to suppliers of ₹214, ₹370 and ₹30 had not been presented for payment, (f) deposits of ₹1,542 made on 30 September were cleared by the bank on 2 October, and (g) the bank had wrongly charged a cheque of ₹72 to M/s Adarsh Trading.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. In the amended cash book, the correction in respect of the cheque of ₹47 issued to a supplier is-

options.A: a debit of ₹94
options.B: a debit of ₹47
options.C: a credit of ₹94
options.D: a credit of ₹47

answer_html:
Answer: (C) a credit of ₹94.

The cheque of ₹47 was a payment but was entered as a receipt, so the cash book has been debited with ₹47 where it should have been credited with ₹47. subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A trial balance-

options.A: is an account forming part of the books of account of the entity concerned
options.B: is one of the final statements prepared at the close of the accounting year
options.C: proves the accounting accuracy of the transactions recorded in the books
options.D: is not an account but only a statement of the debit and credit balances of accounts

answer_html:
Answer: (D) is not an account but only a statement of the debit and credit balances of accounts.

A trial balance is a list of debit and credit balances extracted from the various ledger accounts. It is not an account but only a statement of the debit and credit balances of accounts, and it is not a part of the final statements. It establishes the arithmetical accuracy of the transactions recorded, but it does not prove accounting accuracy, which can be determined only by audit. It also does not form part of the books of account, being a report prepared by extracting balances from them.

Among their features are that they are a special type of journal entry, that there are no source documents such as vouchers for the transactions, that they are recorded in the Journal Proper, that they are passed to comply with accounting principles, and that they are passed at the end of an accounting period. subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A bad debt and a doubtful debt are respectively a debt-

options.A: confirmed to be uncollectible, and one the collectability of which is not certain
options.B: the collectability of which is not certain, and one confirmed to be uncollectible
options.C: which is likely to be realised in full, and one confirmed to be uncollectible
options.D: confirmed to be uncollectible, and one which is likely to be realised in full

answer_html:
Answer: (A) confirmed to be uncollectible, and one the collectability of which is not certain.

On the basis of the chances of collection, debts are classified into good debts, which are likely to be realised in full, bad debts, which are confirmed to be uncollectible or irrecoverable and are therefore a confirmed loss, and doubtful debts, the collectability of which is not certain owing to factors such as the customer becoming insolvent.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The provision for doubtful debts is shown in the balance sheet-

options.A: as a deduction from sundry creditors
options.B: as a deduction from sundry debtors
options.C: on the liabilities side under provisions
options.D: as an addition to sundry debtors

answer_html:
Answer: (B) as a deduction from sundry debtors.

The provision for doubtful debts is shown as a deduction from the sundry debtors in the balance sheet of the entity, and the provision for discount on debtors is likewise deducted from the resulting figure. A provision is defined as a charge against profit for the purpose of providing for any liability or loss and is an internal non-cash expense.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: A bad debt written off in an earlier year and recovered during the current year is-

options.A: shown as a deduction from the bad debts of the current year
options.B: directly credited to the Profit and Loss Account
options.C: credited to the Sundry Debtors Account of the party
options.D: credited to the Provision for Doubtful Debts Account

answer_html:
Answer: (B) directly credited to the Profit and Loss Account.

A bad debt written off in any earlier year, if recovered during the current year, is directly credited to the Profit and Loss Account. It is not credited to the debtor's account, since that account was closed when the debt was written off as irrecoverable.

subject: Fundamentals of Financial and Cost Accounting
question_html: The provision for discount on debtors is calculated on the balance of sundry debtors after adjusting-

options.A: nothing at all, the provision being calculated on the gross figure of sundry debtors
options.B: bad debts, provision for doubtful debts and discount allowed
options.C: bad debts and discount allowed, but before the provision for doubtful debts
options.D: the provision for doubtful debts alone, bad debts having already been written off

answer_html:
Answer: (B) bad debts, provision for doubtful debts and discount allowed.

The provision for doubtful debts is calculated on the balance of sundry debtors after adjusting the further bad debts appearing outside the trial balance. The provision for discount on debtors is calculated on the balance of sundry debtors after adjusting bad debts, the provision for doubtful debts and discount allowed, so that no discount is provided on the portion already regarded as doubtful.
